description: Word Usage is a crucial component of Verbal Ability. It tests a candidate's ability to understand the various meanings, grammatical roles, and contextual applications of a specific word.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.description: Many words in the English language have multiple meanings. Their exact meaning depends entirely on the context of the sentence in which they are used.

key_concepts.explanation: These are words that have the same spelling and pronunciation but completely different meanings. Example: 'Bank' (side of a river) and 'Bank' (financial institution).
These are words that have the same pronunciation but different spellings and meanings. Example: 'Piece' (a portion) and 'Peace' (tranquility).
A specific group of words that naturally go together in English. For example, we say 'Make a mistake', not 'Do a mistake'.

sections.title: Question Types
sections.description: In competitive exams, Word Usage questions are presented in various formats to assess the depth of a candidate's vocabulary and contextual understanding.

question_types.type_name: Multiple Usage of a Single Word
question_types.explanation: A main word is given and used in 3-4 different sentences. You have to identify in which sentences the word has been used correctly or incorrectly.
question_types.approach: Analyze the Parts of Speech and the contextual meaning of the word in each sentence. Check if the usage makes logical and grammatical sense.

question_types.explanation: Four or five different sentences are provided, each highlighting a specific word. You must select the sentence where the word is used incorrectly.
question_types.approach: This error is generally related to grammar or collocation. Pay special attention to the prepositions attached to the word.

sections.title: Confusing Words (Paronyms)
sections.description: Exams frequently test words that look or sound almost identical but have vastly different meanings and grammatical applications.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The new policy will have a bad affect on the economy.
examples.correct_or_usage: The new policy will have a bad effect on the economy.
examples.explanation: 'Affect' is a verb meaning 'to influence'. 'Effect' is a noun meaning 'result or impact'. A noun was required here.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The school principle gave a speech.
examples.correct_or_usage: The school principal gave a speech.
examples.explanation: 'Principal' refers to the head of a school or the most important thing. 'Principle' refers to a fundamental rule or belief.

examples.incorrect_or_context: He is completely disinterested in watching the movie.
examples.correct_or_usage: He is completely uninterested in watching the movie.
examples.explanation: 'Disinterested' means 'impartial or unbiased', whereas 'uninterested' means 'not wanting to learn more about something or not caring'.

sections.title: Context and Tone Indicators
sections.description: To identify the exact meaning of any word, it is essential to study the tone of the sentence and the surrounding words.

key_indicators.usage_hint: Identify the subject of the sentence. 'Capital' means 'chief city' in Geography, whereas it means 'financial assets' in Economics.
These words indicate the direction of the sentence. If 'Although' is used, the second part of the sentence will require a word with an opposing meaning.

sections.title: Strategies for Solving
sections.description: Crucial strategies to solve Word Usage questions within the time limit and with high accuracy.

strategies.title: Identify Parts of Speech
strategies.detail: Read the sentence and determine whether the blank or highlighted word requires a Noun, Verb, Adjective, or Adverb. Many incorrect options can be eliminated based on this alone.

strategies.title: Substitution Technique
strategies.detail: If you are unsure about a word's usage, try replacing it with its simplest synonym. If the sentence still makes logical sense, the original usage is likely correct.

strategies.title: Elimination Method
strategies.detail: In Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs), immediately eliminate options where the word usage is blatantly incorrect grammatically or contextually. This narrows down the choices and increases accuracy.

exceptions.explanation: Sometimes a word does not follow general grammatical rules or its literal meaning because it is part of an idiom or fixed expression.
exceptions.example: He decided to 'table' the proposal. (Here, 'table' does not mean the piece of furniture, but rather 'to postpone' or 'suspend consideration').
